The central question is: when you extend a transformer's context window far beyond the sequence lengths it was trained on, how do the attention sink positions behave — do they remain stable, migrate to new positions, or fragment — and does that shift break downstream layer representations in ways that degrade coherence? Attention sinks are the small set of token positions (almost always early absolute positions) that accumulate disproportionate softmax probability mass from most heads across most layers, acting as a kind of "garbage collection" valve that lets heads avoid attending to irrelevant content without numerical instability. Under distribution shift from extended context, the worry is not that accuracy degrades smoothly and gracefully — it's that sink migration can be discontinuous: a head that silently re-anchors its sink to a different position mid-sequence will corrupt the residual stream of every layer above it in ways that look like unrelated failures (repetition, topic drift, hallucination) with no obvious causal trace. What beginners miss is that sinks are not an architectural feature — they are an emergent equilibrium that RoPE, ALiBi, or other position encodings help sustain, and extending context changes the positional geometry in ways that can destabilize that equilibrium non-uniformly across heads and layers. The expert worry is specifically about cross-layer propagation: a sink shift in layer 8 doesn't stay in layer 8; it feeds a corrupted key/value representation into layer 9, which may then develop a secondary spurious sink, creating a cascade that is extremely difficult to diagnose because each layer looks locally plausible.

NEXT: If sink positions are an emergent equilibrium rather than a designed feature, what specific property of the training loss surface causes early absolute positions to win that equilibrium — and does that property weaken, hold, or invert as context length scales?

The core property is initialization asymmetry compounded by early gradient dominance: during training on short sequences, the first one or two tokens receive attention from every subsequent position at every layer from the very first forward pass, meaning they accumulate far more gradient signal than any other position and their key/value projections are shaped by that pressure into "universally attendable" representations. Xiao et al. (2023) in the StreamingLLM paper quantified this directly — in LLaMA and Pythia models, removing just the first four tokens from the KV cache caused perplexity to spike dramatically even when thousands of other tokens remained, confirming that these positions carry load disproportionate to their semantic content. The reason early absolute positions win over, say, semantically rich tokens is that softmax attention has a numerical pressure toward uniformity when no position is clearly relevant — and early tokens are the only positions that have been "seen attending to" by every layer during every training step, making them the lowest-cost sink across the entire loss landscape. With RoPE specifically, this equilibrium is supported by the fact that small absolute position indices produce near-zero rotational displacement between query and key vectors, making early tokens cheap to attend to from any distance; Су et al.'s original RoPE paper shows that the inner product between rotated vectors decays with relative distance, so position 0 and 1 are geometrically privileged under any query. The critical scaling question is that this property weakens but does not simply invert: as context length extends beyond training distribution, the rotational geometry for large position indices becomes extrapolated and unreliable, which initially reinforces the sink at early positions (nothing else is trustworthy), but past some threshold the model begins encountering position indices so far out-of-distribution that even the early-position advantage can't stabilize attention, and heads start distributing mass erratically — which is exactly what Liu et al. (2023) observed in "Lost in the Middle" as a functional collapse rather than a clean failure mode.

Positional interpolation generically compresses the rotation frequencies, which has a subtle but important effect on sink geometry: by mapping a longer context into the original position index range, you preserve the relative decay profile but flatten the absolute magnitude of rotational displacement at every position — meaning early tokens remain the least-displaced, but the gap between early and mid-sequence positions shrinks, making the privileged status of position 0–1 less extreme. YaRN (Peng et al., 2023) partially addresses this by using non-uniform frequency scaling — high-frequency dimensions are interpolated more aggressively while low-frequency dimensions are left near-original — which empirically preserves perplexity better than linear interpolation (they report recovery to near-baseline at 128k tokens on LLaMA-2), but the mechanism implicitly relies on the low-frequency dimensions continuing to provide the long-range decay that anchors sink behavior, and this is never explicitly verified per-head. LongRoPE (Ding et al., 2024) goes further by searching per-layer, per-dimension rescaling factors, and their ablations show that uniform rescaling causes more attention head "drift" than the searched non-uniform factors — which is indirect evidence that naive interpolation does destabilize sinks in at least a subset of heads. The dangerous regime is moderate interpolation ratios (2x–8x): at these scales, the compression is enough to make positions 10–50 geometrically closer to position 0 than they were during training, which can cause secondary sink candidates to emerge at semantically salient early positions like the first punctuation mark or the first content token — a fragmentation pattern that is distinct from clean migration and harder to detect. Beyond roughly 16x interpolation without fine-tuning, multiple groups (including the LongRoPE authors and the Mistral long-context reports) observe what amounts to sink multiplicity: several heads simultaneously maintain competing high-mass positions, which produces the cross-layer corruption cascade described earlier because layers disagree about which position is the "drain" for irrelevant attention mass.

The honest answer is that direct mechanistic evidence is thin, but the indirect evidence strongly favors tolerance over re-consolidation: models like Llama-3.1 and Mistral large that were fine-tuned on long-context data (128k+ tokens) still show multiple high-mass attention positions when you probe their attention maps at long contexts, rather than converging back to a clean position-0 dominant pattern, suggesting the fine-tuning taught the residual stream to function despite distributional sink load rather than eliminating the competition. The key mechanistic signature that would distinguish the two outcomes is the cross-layer correlation structure of sink positions: in a true re-consolidation, you would expect layer N's top-mass position to predict layer N+1's top-mass position with high consistency (a stable chain), whereas in tolerance you would expect each layer to have its own locally stable high-mass position that is partially decorrelated from adjacent layers — and the MLP sublayers would show compensatory activation patterns that correct for the inter-layer disagreement rather than passing a clean signal forward. Anthropic's attention head analysis work and similar probing studies (e.g., Olsson et al.'s induction head paper, 2022) established the toolkit for this kind of cross-layer consistency measurement, but it hasn't been applied specifically to the sink-multiplicity-after-finetuning question as of mid-2024 literature. A concrete distinguishing experiment would be to measure the mutual information between layer i and layer i+k's argmax attention position as a function of k, across base vs. interpolation-only vs. long-context-finetuned model variants: re-consolidation predicts MI stays high across all k, tolerance predicts MI decays with k but the model's task performance remains intact because MLPs have absorbed the correction burden. The practical implication of tolerance is alarming: it means long-context fine-tuning may be silently loading the MLP layers with a stabilization task they weren't trained for at short contexts, which would explain the consistent empirical observation that long-context fine-tuned models show degraded performance on short-context benchmarks — a phenomenon reported by the Llama long-context team and others but typically attributed vaguely to "catastrophic forgetting" rather than this specific mechanistic shift.

Mechanistic interpretability work on GPT-2 and LLaMA-class models (Geva et al., 2022 on MLP layers as "memory"; Heimersheim & Nanda, 2024 on residual stream composition) consistently shows that early MLPs handle low-level feature binding and middle MLPs handle relational/contextual integration, so the correction burden for a positional artifact like sink migration would fall on the middle MLPs because they are the first layers capable of representing "which position is currently acting as drain" as an abstract feature. AdaLoRA (Zhang et al., 2023) demonstrated the general principle that importance-weighted rank allocation outperforms uniform rank on standard benchmarks, using singular value decomposition of weight update matrices to dynamically redistribute rank budget — but AdaLoRA's importance metric is gradient magnitude, which would correctly identify middle layers as high-importance under long-context fine-tuning if the training signal is long-context data, making it a candidate off-the-shelf solution that has simply never been explicitly evaluated for sink-correction specifically. An optimally layer-heterogeneous strategy for this failure mode would have three zones: low rank (4–8) on attention and MLP in layers 0–25% (early layers where positional features are being set and little correction is needed), high rank (32–64) on MLP up/down projections specifically in layers 25–60% (the sink-correction zone), and moderate rank (16) on attention output projections in layers 60–100% (where late-layer retrieval and coherence adaptation happens but not positional correction). The key non-obvious design choice is to apply LoRA asymmetrically within a layer — specifically targeting MLP down-projections more heavily than up-projections in the middle zone, because the down-projection is where the corrective "write" back to the residual stream happens and is therefore the proximal site of the adaptation. The practical obstacle is that this strategy requires either a pilot run to localize the sink-correction zone per model (since the 25–60% estimate will shift with architecture depth and head count), or a cheap proxy signal like attention entropy variance across layers at long context — which could be computed in a single forward pass on a diagnostic batch before allocating the rank budget, making this a feasible two-stage fine-tuning protocol rather than a theoretical ideal.

Attention entropy variance is computable at inference time with negligible overhead — it requires no additional parameters, just a running statistics buffer over the attention weight tensors that are already materialized — and the signal is fast enough to be meaningful: a spike in cross-layer entropy variance at a given sequence position is detectable within a single forward pass, giving you a per-token diagnostic that flags when the model is entering the instability regime before the residual stream corruption has fully propagated. The most concrete inference-time intervention that doesn't require fine-tuning is attention sink anchoring, which StreamingLLM (Xiao et al., 2023) already demonstrated in a limited form: by forcibly retaining the first four tokens in the KV cache regardless of recency, they prevented sink eviction and recovered near-baseline perplexity at streaming lengths — this is effectively a hard constraint that freezes the sink position, and it works precisely because it prevents migration rather than correcting it after the fact. A more sophisticated intervention would be entropy-triggered attention logit adjustment: when cross-layer entropy variance exceeds a threshold (empirically, something like 2x the variance observed at training-distribution lengths), you apply a learned or heuristic additive bias to the attention logits of the designated sink positions to restore their dominance — this is similar in spirit to the "attention temperature scaling" used in some long-context inference optimizations, but targeted specifically at sink positions rather than applied globally. The fundamental limitation of any inference-time correction without weight updates is that you can stabilize the attention pattern but you cannot fix the residual stream values that have already been corrupted by earlier-layer sink disagreement — so the intervention has a temporal horizon problem: it works if applied before corruption propagates (detectable ~2–4 layers before failure in typical cascades based on residual stream analysis literature), but fails if the diagnostic lags the instability. A practical architecture for this would combine the entropy diagnostic with a layer-wise KV cache intervention: cache the attention output at the last stable layer (identified by the entropy signal dropping back below threshold), and if instability is detected in subsequent layers, revert the residual stream contribution from those layers by blending with the cached stable state — essentially a soft rollback that trades some representational fidelity for positional stability, at a compute cost of roughly one additional attention operation per flagged layer.

This is the central tension that makes the soft rollback idea fragile: the residual stream at any given layer is a superposition of corruption and correction, and a naive revert to an earlier state throws away both simultaneously — which is worse than doing nothing if the MLP correction signal is larger in magnitude than the attention corruption signal, a condition that is entirely plausible in a model that has been long-context fine-tuned precisely to build those corrections. The mechanistic interpretability framing that makes this precise is the linear representation hypothesis applied to the residual stream: if attention-induced corruption and MLP-induced correction are approximately linearly separable directions in residual stream space, then the right intervention is not a rollback but a targeted projection that removes the corruption direction while preserving the correction direction — and this is in principle computable if you have a probe trained to identify the "sink instability" direction, analogous to how activation steering work (Zou et al., 2023; Turner et al., 2023) subtracts specific concept directions from residual streams at inference time. The practical obstacle is that the corruption and correction directions are unlikely to be cleanly orthogonal — the MLP correction is specifically shaped in response to the corruption, meaning they share subspace, and projecting out the corruption direction will partially destroy the correction by construction, with the degree of entanglement being an empirical question that hasn't been measured for this specific case. A concrete way to bound the problem is to compare layer ablation experiments on long vs. short context: if ablating middle-layer MLPs (zeroing their output) causes larger perplexity degradation at long context than short context, that directly measures how much correction load they are carrying, and the magnitude of that differential tells you how much you'd lose in a rollback — Geva et al.'s (2022) MLP ablation methodology on GPT-2 provides the exact template for this experiment. The uncomfortable conclusion is that for a model that has been heavily fine-tuned on long context, the soft rollback is probably net-negative, while for a base model with only positional interpolation applied, it may still be net-positive — which means the right inference-time strategy is model-class conditional: detect whether the model has internalized MLP correction (via a cheap calibration pass measuring MLP ablation sensitivity differential) and only apply rollback if it hasn't, otherwise fall back to the logit-adjustment-only intervention that leaves the residual stream untouched.
